newsitem.title: USA: Container ship still stuck on Florida reef.
newsitem.headline: Container ship still stuck on Florida reef.

text.p: Legal wrangling delayed until Saturday efforts to free a 600 foot (182.9 metres) container ship grounded on a patch of coral and sand in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, U.S. officials said on Friday.
Salvage experts, operating under the watchful eye of the Coast Guard and park officials, were scheduled to transfer 540,000 gallons (2.044 million litres) of fuel to a specially equipped barge.

The plan was to make the Mexican-flagged ship lighter so it would float higher and a tugboat could drag it free at high tide. Officials said late on Friday that the earliest the attempt -- planned for high tide on Friday evening -- would be made would be on Saturday.
Work to free the container ship was also delayed by at least a day because of legal maneuvering between two salvage companies over responsibility in the event of a fuel spill.

"It is no simple matter to bring a fuel barge into a national marine sanctuary," said Matt Bokor, a spokesman for ECM Hudson of Camden, New Jersey, the marine consulting firm in charge of the salvage team.
"I'm certain (liability) was one of the considerations. I wouldn't say it was the only one," he added.
Efforts to free the ship, called the Houston, were also delayed because of problems assembling a crew for a tugboat, he said.
Officials said the Mexican owners of the ship were cooperating in the salvage effort and had taken responsibility for the incident.
"The owners of the vessel have accepted responsibility for the grounding and are providing all the necessary personnel to refloat the vessel," said Coast Guard spokesman Marcus Woodring.
The container ship, owned by the freight company Transportation Maritima Mexicana, hit the fragile coral reef late on Sunday. The owners were not available to comment on the grounding.
Once the Houston is pulled free, it will be towed to an anchorage site on the open sea where divers will inspect its hull for signs of damage.
So far, none of the ship's 810,000 gallons (3.066 million litres) of fuel has leaked.

The ship ran aground on an ancient coral reef that was covered by the rising sea millions of years ago, said marine biologist Ben Haskell of the sanctuary. New corals are growing on the reef and the area is made up of 20 percent living coral, he said.

Coast Guard inspectors discovered earlier this week that one of the ship's engine cylinders was cracked. They suspect the damage occurred as the crew struggled to free the ship, a Coast Guard spokesman said.
After the grounding, the crew battled for hours to free the ship and did not report the incident until dawn on Monday, which violated U.S. law, according to a Coast Guard spokesman.
Ships are required to report groundings in U.S. waters immediately so the Coast Guard can monitor salvage efforts to ensure no more damage is done.
